blocks.x: This is the first reel. We're just starting off today. Oh, yeah. And let's get your name first. My name is Jesse Charles. That's your full name? Uh-huh. You don't have any middle name at all? Uh-huh. All right. Now, yours?
Judy Pushker.

Martin Sher. And I'm Dick Allen. All right. So, let's see. What's today's date? It's December the... What is it? Um... Today. December the 15th on the newspaper. Yes. Bill of Rights Day. That's right. I read that. Up at school. See, I got some stuff. Oh, you got it all written down.
I got a little jot down here. Not much of it.
Yeah. Well, let's start at the beginning. You know, you can tell us when you were born and where.

I remember when I was born. You were born? Yeah. I was born in 1900. And raised in Louisiana. And I started to play. And my first job was with my brother. He was sitting in his band. Cornbread. You remember? You know Cornbread. Yeah. Cornbread used to play with my brother.
Well, is Cornbread from Raceline?

Well, he's from here. But my brother, he came down here after we got grown, you know? Mm-hmm. But anyway, my first job was with my brother. He's sitting in his band. And we used to play house parties, lawn parties, and dance hall jobs, and so on. And my first big break was with Jack Carey's band. I didn't know what the job was paying, but Jack gave me $15 that day. I was on the count of a day. That was Aiden Franklin. This was in 1926. Now, I, after that, I left here in 28. And, uh, we went to Monroe, Louisiana, to play a labor dance. I, uh, came back, I stayed there. I came back in 39. Yeah, I stayed there until 39. And when I came back, it was big band days. I, uh...
We can turn it off. We were talking about big band days. Yeah, huh?
We came back to the city. Yeah, this was in the 39th when I came back. It said they didn't tell 39. You got it on?
I wanted to ask you something. We got the second reel going. We're gone for 30 minutes. I didn't ask you how you spell your name.
J-E-S-S-I-E. Jesse Charles. I thought it was with an I-E. Some people spell the name J-E-S-I-E. I put an I to my...
She was asking you about the zoos. Have you ever seen it?
Names of Constance. Wait, let's back up. That was the biology. Okay. What about the Zulu Parades?

The Zulu Parades. Well, they have their big parades on the count of them. They have Zulu Parades during the summertime, too. They have one or two parades. But they have big days on the count of them. Just like last day on the count of them, that's when they have their big days. They have floats like Rex and them. They don't have as many of them, but they have a few of them. They be right in there, too. They have different routes from Rex and around there, different sections of town they go to. And everybody will be on the lookout for them. They will be out there. They have a lot of coconuts to give away.
What is a parade that dresses up like Indians?

Well, that's just an Indian parade. I mean, they don't have what you call a parade. It's just a group of them get together and just parade them down the streets themselves. But they don't have what you call a parade. They have certain places they'll meet. A group of them from downtown, they might meet a group uptown. See, like early in the morning you might hear them passing, or they might be on their way uptown to meet another group, certain places they meet. And then there's just a few of them, a group of them get together and just stroll the street in Indians. But they're pretty. They're really pretty. They're really pretty. They would say it would cost some money. But they have... They're not accompanied by bands?
Huh? Are they accompanied by bands?

No, they don't have no bands. No, they don't have no bands. They got their little song they sing and they pat their hand like the rail in them. They do their little dance, you know? That's where they get their kids. They're not bad like they used to. It used to be rough. They used to fight a lot. So I mean like downtown, we would meet the group uptown. The chief didn't bow to them, they'd have a fight. But now, now they don't fight like the Indians.
What do they fight with?

Well, they wouldn't have knives or anything. They just had their little spears, you know, like the railings. If one of the guys uptown wouldn't bow until the guys from downtown, well, they'd be a fight.
Did they ever have bows and arrows? I never saw them.

No, well they have, I don't say bows and arrows, but they have their little spears, you know, their hair, imitation, and things like that. But they're not rough like they used to play. But they're pretty to look at. They really have some pretty suits there. Yeah.
You said about uptown and downtown. Was there always the same between the two groups?

Down, yeah, uh-huh. Yeah, uh-huh. Well, that's the way some people feel about it. I mean, a guy live way downtown, a guy live uptown. I mean, he has his group and the guy down in town have his group, you know? Uh-huh. Tell me that a long time ago, years ago, I mean, like if you live way downtown and you couldn't go uptown, you couldn't hardly go up there. This guy would tear you up. It's not like that now. Yeah. Did you ever play around the big 25s or beat-luck? No, I heard of that. That was before my time. 25. That was before my time. I heard it at 25.
But did you play mostly uptown when you first came here?

Yeah, because I was living uptown at that time. Doing my brother sitting at that time before he started out. Uh-huh. Yeah, we used to play uptown mostly. I would job uptown. And we played a lot of jobs downtown, too. Where at? Well, most of our job when we started out, when I started out at my brother Sidney, well, like I said, it was mostly party jobs and dance hall jobs. We'd play out in the lake, you know, like that, and excretion yards, like that.
Different places like that. Did you ever play around customizing the basin? No, no, no. Where all the fast women were in? No, no, no.

I remember those days. I remember those days. I remember those days. But that was before my time. Yeah, before my time. Yeah, I remember Basin Street. All down in the district. But that was before my time. I had to start playing there. Did they have many bands in the district when you were here? Yeah, they had quite a few bands. I mean, like Buddy Petit. Well, they was playing different places. They had bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo band at the time.
Did they play in the Red Light District though? Did you ever see them down there?

Kid Punching them? No, I never saw them down there. I used to see Willie Irmfree, I used to see them at the Larrick Cabaret. I used to go to the Larrick Cabaret. They had the old Larrick Theater down in the street. They used to have what you call Larrick Cabaret. They had a cabaret down below underneath the theater. They had a nightclub called Cabaret. I remember Willie Irmfree, Punch taking me there. The first time I went there, Punch taking me there. He was my homeboy quite nice. He used to take me around and when we'd go in places like that, he'd say, well this is my clarinet player. I didn't even know how to play at that time, but he would just tell the people that they'd get me in. They didn't know what they knew him. So anyway, we went to see Willie Irmfree. I remember that a long time ago.
You know, we forgot to ask him something, what he played when he was in the brass bands.

No, he didn't play that. No, he didn't play that. I was playing tenor when I first started the brass band. I was playing tenor saxophone. I don't know what I was doing. John Kasman, George. And later on when I began to fool around with Dixieland, I mean I got an interest in winning the Dixieland band here late these late years, I picked up my clarinet again. And I played a few jobs on the clarinet with Abby Williams and guys like that. But the more it was my clarinet job I went to tenor.
I remember one job you played clarinet on because we went a special kind of job to send Kid Sheik off. Yeah, yeah, yeah. And they had a brass band at the train station. Yeah, yeah, yeah.

It's a different kind of job. That's right. That's more of a donation. Like when they play, you know, send guys off or go meet guys like that. But I know that's more of a donation. If you want to go, you know, just donate your service like that. It's okay. Just like a lot of funerals we play. A lot of funerals we play for different members, you know, union guys. It's okay. It's just if you want to donate your service. Yeah, it's okay. Yeah. And we donate our service to George Williams and John Casmick. And it wasn't paid. Do you get paid for fuel? No, just donate your service. Just something free would give them. And it wasn't paid. Because he was a musician, see. Yeah. Well most of the time do you get paid or is it- Oh yeah, most of the time. Like anybody else, I mean, wouldn't be connected with the local. I mean, it's just paid jobs. Yeah. Like all the parade jobs, that's paid jobs. There's no donation there.
Just if you have a good friend and maybe he passed away then for his funeral, you just donate-

Well, sometimes they do that. Like somebody passed in the neighborhood and he'd be a nice guy. Sometimes they just pick up money between the neighbors for the band sometimes. And they pay the band. I mean, lots of cases like that. We play jobs. I mean, people pick up money between their friends and pay for the band because he was a good time guy. But outside of a musician, I don't know any band with donated service. I mean, just to say, well, we play for nothing.
Did you ever see him put a saucer on a guy's chest when he laid out?
No, I heard of that, but I never saw it.
A what? They put a saucer on a guy's chest when he's laid out in his coffin.
That's for people to put money when they come to see him.
Oh! They put a...oh my goodness.
Yeah, I heard of that, but I never saw it. I never saw it. Yeah, I heard of that. I mean, that's been years ago.
It must have been. Years ago, yeah.
And this is also what pays for the funeral and the bank? Is that...? No, the Benevolent Society.

Yeah, he would pay for whatever bill or his funeral, I guess, or something like that. You know, like a fellow don't have enough money to take care of his funeral and he finally had made a big debt for him or something like that. And they say, well, just put a saucer there. Well, that represents that he needs money. And whoever wanted to put money in there, they'd put money in there. I guess when the saucer gets filled, they'd go dump it and put it back there. I heard of that, but I never saw it. That must have been for my time.

Well, how do they get the money for, say, some guy who's a sport, you know, and he didn't have any money? How would his friends collect the money? For what? A funeral? For a funeral. To pay for the band. How do they get that?

Oh, well, they pick up money, like I said, by the neighborhood. Just like it's a good time guy in this neighborhood, or a guy die, get killed, and he'd been a regular guy around the neighborhood. And he don't have enough money to have a band, see? Maybe the family can't. He's not able to pay for bands, see? Well, some guy, a good time guy, maybe some of his friends say, well, man, we're going to pick up some money. We come around to my door, around the neighbors, each door like that, or a ballroom, and pick up so much money, and pick up a band. That's where they pay. Yeah, we pay lots of jobs, like that.
Do they have certain prices, or just whatever the donation is?

No, it's a certain price for the band, and they'll pick up that amount of money. Yeah. I guess whatever it's like, and I guess maybe some bigger guy would say, well, I'll pay the rest of them. Like some guy hanging around the ballroom all the time, a good time guy. Maybe it might be some guy running a ballroom or some business place. When he dies, he don't have enough. So the guy didn't have a good time with him, so we won't see them having a band. And he's like, that second line, they enjoy that, see? Yeah, they enjoy that. That's the life of a parade in a funeral, of all. The second line, and that's the life of a parade, any kind of parade, the second line.
How would you define a second line? Huh? How would you define a second line?

Well, the second line is people just on the side, see? Like if you're having a parade, the members be in the middle of the street with the band, see? They'll be walking, and the second line be on the side. Well, they get the kick out of that. They'll be dancing and clowning and drinking in the street and be walking. They call that the second line, see? But that's the life of the parade, the second line. Yeah, that's the life of the parade. It gets pretty rough sometimes, you know? It gets full of wine and it kills them a lot. But, uh, it don't get too rough, it's good because it's alive. You see them on TV, I mean, that's the show of the second line.
What do they do besides drink wine? Do any of them smoke?
I imagine so. I imagine they do everything to get a kick. Anything to get a kick?
Yeah, I imagine so. Yeah. Yeah, I imagine so. What about needles? Do they fool with that? I imagine all that goes.

I never have seen them. Me either. I never saw a guy. I've never been around people smoke that stuff and never been around people use that dope. No kind of way. But I heard of it. It's just something that gave me a different kind of feeling.
Some of those second lines look awful funny.
Well, there's no telling what they do. I'm telling them that that second line is, you see some characters out there. Yeah, this is out there, this is out there for anything. Yeah.
Have you ever been in the Trim May section?
The what?
Trim May section.
No.
Where'd she just come to, just came to? No, she's from Uptown. They live Uptown. Yeah. Up near the school. Yeah. Yeah.
Oh, I thought maybe she just came here.

She doesn't know much about downtown. Oh. Well, see a lot of funerals that he played started from around Gresseline and Robinson. Yeah, yeah. And they'd have a particular group of second liners that hung around there and a lot of, well, Roof's Cozy Corner is one of the main places. Yeah, yeah. That's right. I don't know if Ruth puts up any money or so.

Oh, yeah, Ruth, yeah. Yeah, Ruth, she's a big time broad man. There she go with that. Yeah, she had her club turned out here, a couple of, about a month or so ago. Yeah, see they have a club. Yeah, they have a club. We played her first parade. I was with Abby that Abby got a job. Abby Williams?
Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. That's been about three years ago, two years ago.
Well, they have the Cozy Corner door poppers. Tell them what a door popper is.
Oh, door popper. Door popper. Just people like to peep through the windows and doors and interfere with other people's business. And, you know, just bad. Like a peep in town.
Yeah.
Like a gossip. You know women that gossip, you know?
Yeah.
I hope you're better than that. Gossip, yeah.
Henry Allen, young Henry Allen, he's from the other side.

Let me say this is Jesse Charles, the third reel, just so we can keep it straight in case they get mixed up in the boxes. I'm just saying what reel we're on now in case they get mixed up in the boxes. We never did finish with the cornerstones, what kind of organization is there, society?
Baptist Church is mostly going to have that. Yeah, Baptist Church is mostly going to have that.
Cornerstone land.
I'll start again if you're ready. This is Reel 4, Jesse Charles. We were talking about the parades that they had before the menstrual show to advertise.

Uh-huh, yeah. Well, like I said before, I played one parade on a public ministry show during that season. And the next season I didn't go back on account of those parades they were making, but a few years later I went back and they had cut the parades out. And the only thing you had to do on that show was to play the showdown. And that was alright because you'd rehearse for three weeks and get the showdown.

segments.title: Reel opening, names and date
segments.summary: Introductions of interviewee and interviewers, and the date, 15 December.

segments.title: Born 1900; first jobs with brother and Jack Carey, leaving 1928, return 1939
segments.summary: Charles was born in 1900 in Louisiana, first played in his brother's band at house parties and dance halls, got a break with Jack Carey's band in 1926, left in 1928 for Monroe and came back in 1939.

segments.title: Second reel begins; spelling of his name
segments.summary: Second reel starts and Charles spells his name.

segments.title: Zulu parades and floats
segments.summary: Charles describes the Zulu parades, their big days, floats and routes.

segments.title: Mardi Gras Indians, their songs and fights
segments.summary: He explains the Indian groups who parade without bands, their songs and spears, and how uptown and downtown chiefs used to fight.

segments.title: Uptown versus downtown rivalry
segments.summary: Groups from uptown and downtown used to be rivals, and he never played the Big 25s.

segments.title: Playing uptown with his brother Sidney
segments.summary: He played mostly uptown, with some downtown, in party, dance hall, lake and excursion jobs for his brother's band.

segments.title: Basin Street and the district bands
segments.summary: Charles remembers Basin Street and the district as before his time, and mentions Buddy Petit among the bands (the transcript degenerates into a repeated-word ASR loop).

segments.title: Kid Punch taking him to the Lyric Cabaret
segments.summary: His homeboy Kid Punch took him to the Lyric Cabaret and introduced him as his clarinet player before he could play.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and second lines
segments.title: Tenor sax in brass bands, later back to clarinet
segments.summary: He played tenor saxophone in brass bands, later picked up clarinet again for Dixieland jobs with Abby Williams, though mostly stayed on tenor.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and second lines
segments.title: Donated services versus paid jobs
segments.summary: Brass band jobs like seeing off Kid Sheik or funerals for musicians are donated, while parades and most jobs are paid.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and second lines
segments.title: The saucer on the coffin and benevolent societies
segments.summary: He has heard of putting a saucer on a laid-out man's chest for donations toward funeral costs but never saw it.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and second lines
segments.title: Neighbourhood collections to pay for a funeral band
segments.summary: Friends and neighbours pick up money to hire a band for a good-time guy's funeral, at a set band price.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and second lines
segments.title: The second line: dancing, drinking and drugs
segments.summary: He defines the second line as the people on the side who are the life of a parade, drinking and clowning, and says he has never seen drug use.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and second lines
segments.title: Funerals near Gresseline and Robinson, Ruth's Cozy Corner and her club
segments.summary: Sher recalls funerals starting near Ruth's Cozy Corner with local second liners, and Charles recalls playing Ruth's club's first parade with Abby Williams.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and second lines
segments.title: What a door popper is
segments.summary: A door popper is a gossip who peeps through windows and doors.

segments.title: Third reel: Henry Allen and benevolent societies
segments.summary: Reel 3 begins with a remark about Henry Allen and a question on which organizations are involved, answered as mostly Baptist churches.

segments.title: Minstrel show parades and showdown rehearsals
segments.summary: On reel 4, he recalls playing one advertising parade for a minstrel show, later the parades were cut and only the show remained after three weeks of rehearsal.
